title: Observed surface radiation and temperature impacts from the large-scale deployment of photovoltaics in the barren area of Gonghe, China
abstract: As the installation of large-scale photovoltaic (PV) facilities in the barren area of Gonghe, China, would cover a substantial portion of the Earth's surface with PV panels, concerns exist about the extent to which PV plants induce unfavorable surface radiative effects from the change in land use. In contrast to the theoretical calculations and model simulations of previous studies, parallel observations derived from in situ experiments spanning two contrasting land surfaces in Gonghe, consisting of a natural barren surface and one covered with PV panel, provide new insight into the potential impact of large-scale PV plants on the surface radiation and temperature. The novel results presented here are as follows. (1) The specific variations of the surface shortwave radiation components enable the PV panels to serve as energy sinks throughout the whole year, especially in the warm season. (2) The cooling of the land surface associated with the PV plant is related to the physical shading by the PV panels and the solar energy conversion. (3) The enhanced temperature of the surface of the PV panel heats the adjacent ambient air, which may subsequently drive a PV heat-island effect. Moreover, recommendations for an improved experimental design are presented. Our findings provide a solid basis for the parameterization of a PV plant in numerical models, with the view to delivering a more realistic quantitative and practical guidance for the development of the solar industry in the future.

## Accepted Manuscript

Observed Surface Radiation and Temperature Impacts from the Large-Scale Deployment of Photovoltaics in the Barren Area of Gonghe, China

Rui Chang, Yanbo Shen, Yong Luo, Bo Wang, Zhenbin Yang, Peng Guo

PII: S0960-1481(17)31108-4 DOI: 10.1016/j.renene.2017.11.007 Reference: RENE 9409 To appear in: Renewable Energy Received Date: 12 June 2017 Revised Date: 01 October 2017 Accepted Date: 04 November 2017

In this work, we evaluated the surface radiation and temperature impacts empirically with _in situ_

observations in Gonghe and provided new insight to this question. Novel results presented here

are listed as the following three highlights:

- A negative (positive) anomaly of SWUP over PV plant during summertime (wintertime).

- A significant cooler land surface over the PV panels across the whole year.

- A notable daytime heating and a nighttime cooling of the surfaces of PV panels

- A basis for the parameterization of a PV plant in numerical model.

## 1 **Observed Surface Radiation and Temperature Impacts from the Large-Scale** 2 **Deployment of Photovoltaics in the Barren Area of Gonghe, China**

- 13 **Abstract:** As the installation of large-scale photovoltaic (PV) facilities in the barren 14 area of Gonghe, China, would cover a substantial portion of the Earth’s surface with 15 PV panels, concerns exist about the extent to which PV plants induce unfavorable 16 surface radiative effects from the change in land use. In contrast to the theoretical 17 calculations and model simulations of previous studies, parallel observations derived 18 from _in situ_ experiments spanning two contrasting land surfaces in Gonghe, consisting 19 of a natural barren surface and one covered with PV panel, provide new insight into 20 the potential impact of large-scale PV plants on the surface radiation and temperature. 21 The novel results presented here are as follows. (1) The specific variations of the 22 surface shortwave radiation components enable the PV panels to serve as energy sinks 23 throughout the whole year, especially in the warm season. (2) The cooling of the land 24 surface associated with the PV plant is related to the physical shading by the PV 25 panels and the solar energy conversion. (3) The enhanced temperature of the surface 26 of the PV panel heats the adjacent ambient air, which may subsequently drive a PV 27 heat-island effect. Moreover, recommendations for an improved experimental design 28 are presented. Our findings provide a solid basis for the parameterization of a PV 29 plant in numerical models, with the view to delivering a more realistic quantitative 30 and practical guidance for the development of the solar industry in the future. 31 **Key words:** large-scale photovoltaic plant; surface radiation and temperature impacts; 32 _in situ_ observations; barren area; land-use change

- 33

- 34 **1. Introduction**

- 35 As large-scale solar energy is becoming more economically and technically feasible, 36 while also being accompanied by policy support in recent years (Bazilian _et al_ . 2013, 37 Benson _et al_ . 2014, Boeck _et al_ . 2016), significant growth of the solar energy industry 38 has occurred worldwide. In the arid northwestern China’s Gonghe, the Longyangxia 39 hydro-solar photovoltaic (PV) power station, with a capacity of 320 MWp and a 40 surface area of 9.16 km[2] , has been connected to the state grid since the end of 2013 41 (China-Daily, 2014). Installation of a large-scale PV power plant, consisting of many 42 PV arrays, covering substantial portions of the Earth’s surface with dark-colored, 43 sunlight-absorbing panels would likely induce a “local climate” with particular 44 radiative impacts. Therefore, the radiative consequences of large-scale PV

- 45 deployment have received increasing attention in recent years, predominantly through 46 examination of the changes in the surface albedo, local surface radiation, as well as air 47 temperature within a PV facility. For instance, Nemet (2009) compared the reduction 48 of the replacement of fossil fuels with PV power generation, in particular the increase 49 in radiative forcing resulting from the increase in the albedo of PV panels, and found 50 a reduced radiative forcing of roughly a factor of 30. Scherba _et al._ (2011) used a 51 sophisticated building-energy model forced with meteorological data to report that 52 solar PV arrays reduce the daily sensible heat flux of an urban environment by 11% 53 on average. The large-scale PV plant deployed in the Mojave Desert of California, 54 USA, tends to increase the local afternoon 2-m air temperature by 0.4 °C based on the 55 results of simulations with a regional climate model (Millstein and Menon, 2011). 56 Simulations with computational fluid dynamics model indicate that the annual mean 57 air temperature at 2.5 m above ground in the center of a PV field is 1.9 °C greater 58 than the ambient temperature, resulting in a heat-island effect of solar plants 59 (Fthenakis _et al._ , 2013).

- 60 The results of numerical weather predication investigations for Los Angeles show no 61 adverse impacts on the urban heat island from large-scale PV deployment, with 62 currently available solar conversion efficiencies predicting a regional cooling of up to 63 0.2 °C (Taha 2013). Similarly, based on panel-scale energy-balance calculations, the 64 direct influence of a PV installation on the heat-island effect was found to be 65 negligible for Tokyo (Genchi _et al.,_ 2003). Recently, a reduced near-surface air 66 temperature related to the deployment of rooftop PV panels was simulated with a 67 coupled modeling system at the scale of a metropolitan area (Salamanca _et al._ 2016). 68 These studies provide important insights into the potential climate impacts of a large69 scale PV plant. However, the lack of _in situ_ observations implies the local climate or 70 radiative effects presented in the above-mentioned studies are mostly theoretical or 71 model-based. Moreover, the effective reflectivity of a PV panel, which is relevant for 72 its solar conversion efficiency, varies from 0.04 (Solar World, 2010) to 0.05 (Nemet, 73 2009) or even as high as 0.1 (Protogeropoulos and Zachariou, 2010). Therefore, a 74 more observation-based analysis with regard to the effect of large-scale PV plants on 75 the local climate effect should be carried out to improve our understanding of this 76 elusive issue.

- 77 Regarding the impacts of a PV plant on the local climate, only a few studies have 78 been performed based on observational data thus far, such as the experimental 79 measurements recorded in Tucson, USA (Barron-Gafford _et al._ 2016) and Golmud 80 (Yang _et al._ 2015, Gao _et al._ 2016). The field study in Tucson indicated an average 81 increase of the 2.5-m air temperature by 3-4 °C during the nighttime as compared 82 with the surrounding areas (Barron-Gafford _et al._ 2016), which was likely associated 83 with the deployment of the PV plant. In Golmud, a significant positive anomaly of the 84 annual net surface radiation and a cooler air temperature at 10 m were revealed, which 85 is likely also resulting from the deployment of the PV plant (Yang _et al._ , 2015, Gao _et_ 86 _al.,_ 2016). In particular, the 10-m air temperature over the PV plant was roughly 0.11

- 87 -0.56 °C cooler than the land in the absence of a PV plant throughout the whole year

- 88 (Gao _et al.,_ 2016). It is worth noting that Golmud is located in a desert region, 89 whereas the utility-scale PV solar plant examined here (Gonghe) is located mostly on 90 barren ground with sparse vegetation (Fig. 1a and 1c). Areas with different land91 surface properties give diverse fluxes of sensible and latent heat, which in turn affect 92 the turbulent mixing and horizontal advection in the atmospheric boundary layer 93 (Doran _et al._ 1995, Harris _et al._ 2014, Guo _et al._ 2009, Guo _et al._ 2016, Miao _et al._ 94 2017). Since the PV plants in Gonghe and Golmud have been erected on different 95 land-surface types, which give quite a different atmospheric boundary-layer structure, 96 the local climate and radiative impacts from the installation and operation of the 97 large-scale PV plants in the barren area of Gonghe deserve comprehensive research 98 and understanding.

- 99 Our objective is, therefore, to evaluate and quantify the potential climate effects

- 100 resulting from change in land-use cover since the installation of a large-scale PV 101 plant, with a focus on changes in the surface radiative balance, as well as the surface 102 temperature. The possible local impacts are assessed based on the coincident 103 observations from two neighboring _in situ_ sites at the Gonghe PV solar park. Below, 104 section 2 presents the data and methods used here, with the preliminary results shown 105 in section 3. Some limitations of our investigation and recommendations for future 106 work are given in section 4. Finally, some concluding remarks are provided in section 107 5.

- 108

- 109 **2. Methods**

- 110 _2.1 Site description_

- 111 The experiments were conducted at a PV plant within the larger Gonghe solar park 112 (36.136°N, 100.588°E; 2909 m above sea level). Fig. 1 shows the spatial distributions 113 of the two monitoring sites, including site A and site B, and the layout of the solar PV 114 array. The boundaries of the PV array, which are marked by black polygons, have 115 been extracted from Google Earth. To minimize the impacts from the variability in 116 local meteorological conditions, the two experimental sites are located within 0.5 km 117 of each other, with site A inside the solar array, and site B outside (Fig. 1), which 118 represents a PV plant and a natural barren environment, respectively. As the close 119 proximity of site B to the solar array may diminish the air-temperature difference 120 within and outside the solar array, this will be discussed in section 4.3.

- 121 Within the Gonghe PV solar park, the ground-cover type is mostly either barren or 122 sparse vegetation. The nearest automated weather station (“GH” in Fig. 1b) is 123 located 18 km to the north of the two monitoring sites. A wind rose for this 124 meteorological station is displayed to the upper left within Fig. 1b.

- 125 Photos of the experimental set-up are also displayed in Fig. 1. As shown in Fig. 1a, 126 the white four-component radiation sensor at site B is mounted on a cross-arm to 127 ensure the sensor is located above the barren surface. In addition, two temperature 128 probes record the different temperatures between the air and the solar panel. One of

- 129 the probes is mounted with a 6-plate shield fixed on a 3-m metal pole, while the other

- 130 is attached to the back of the solar panel (Fig. 1a).

- 131 To simultaneously observe the surface radiation inside the PV array, a four132 component radiation sensor at site A is also mounted to a 3-m cross-arm, which is 133 positioned just above the PV panels (Fig. 1c). Furthermore, as site A is located in the

- 134 third row of the PV arrays, the observed four-component radiation flux at site A 135 largely represents the radiative features inside the PV array.

- 136 As the PV panels are tilted 34[o] from the horizontal and pointed toward the south, and 137 the distance between two panels is about 7.5 m, approximately 70% and 30% of the 138 ground coverage is attributed to the barren ground and PV panels, respectively, within 139 the solar array. Note that the PV installation was erected at the end of 2013, about 18 140 months prior to the installation of the observation tower.

141

The map shows the spatial distribution of major solar PV areas of solar 145 generation (black polygons) as extracted from Google Earth by the end of 2015.The 146 location of the nearest automated weather station is marked by the GH in upper right 147 corner of the map. The wind rose for Gonghe is also plotted on the upper left of this 148 middle panel (b).

- 149 2.2 _Monitoring equipment & variables_

- 150 Measurements of the surface radiation components, including the downward and 151 upward surface shortwave radiation (SWDOWN and SWUP, respectively), downward 152 and upward surface long-wave radiation (LWDOWN and LWUP, respectively) as 153 well as the net surface radiation (NSR, calculated from the four radiation components) 154 are recorded at both of the two sites with a Campbell Scientific NR01 four-component

- 155 net radiometer (Fig. 2) whose expected accuracy for the daily radiation is within 156 ±10% (http://www.campbellsci.com/nr01). The radiometer is positioned at 10 m 157 above ground at site A and at 3 m above ground at site B. This coincident 158 observations of radiation at the two _in situ_ sites enables determination of the radiation 159 impacts of the PV plant (see the discussion in section 4.2 for further details).

- 160

- 161 **Fig. 2.** Photo of the NR01 four-component net radiation sensor 162 (http://www.campbellsci.com/nr01)

- 163 The air temperature and solar-panel temperature at site B are measured with combined 164 temperature and relative humidity probes (Campbell CS215-L, Fig. 3) whose 165 accuracy is ±0.4°C from +5° to +40°C (http://www.campbellsci.com/cs215-l). The air

- 166 temperature is observed at about 2 m above the natural barren surface, and the solar167 panel temperature is observed behind a solar panel at the same height (Fig. 1a).

168

169 **Fig. 3.** Photo of the CS215-L combined temperature and relative humidity probe 170 (left panel) and with a 6-plate shield (right panel).

- 171 (http://www.campbellsci.com/cs215-l)

- 172 The observations are all recorded at one-hour intervals (one-hour averages) for a time

- 173 period of one year (from May 2015 to April 2016), to characterize the seasonal 174 variation of the sun, as well as the climate extremes associated with hot and cold 175 periods.

## 2.3 _Meteorological data_

- 176

- 177 The meteorological datasets, including monthly precipitation and total cloud cover, 178 for the period of 1985-2016, have been recorded at the automated weather station. 179 The data have been provided by the National Meteorological Information Center of 180 China Meteorological Administration, and are used to provide the climatological 181 characteristics of Gonghe.

- 182 _2.4 Data processing_

- 183 The following quality-control procedures are performed on the original observational 184 data. (1) The radiative observations that exceeding the astronomical radiation are 185 removed. (2) The observed records are removed when the surface radiation from 186 either site A or site B is missing. Since the NSR is directly calculated from the 187 original raw four radiation components (SWDOWN, SWUP, LWDOWN and 188 LWUP), which likely introduces errors into the NSR dataset, the NSR is recomputed 189 from the individual quality-controlled four radiation components. The total daily 190 radiation and mean temperatures are produced for each month and are used to 191 compute the summertime (April to September) and wintertime (October to March) 192 means.

- 193 Since the Earth’s surface temperature is determined by the balance between 194 incoming solar radiation and outgoing infrared radiation, we may deduce the land195 surface temperature (LST) from the downward and upward surface long-wave 196 radiation (Sheng _et al._ 2003; Yang _et al_ . 2015). Given the spatial scales involved, the 197 contribution from sensible heating of the air by the ground is ignored, enabling the

- 198 surface upward long-wave radiation _[L] s_ to be written as:

- 199 _Ls_  _ g  Ts_ 4  (1  _ g_ ) _Ra_ (1)

- 200 where _ g_ is the surface emissivity, __ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, _Ts_ is the LST

- 201 and _[R] a_ is the downward surface long-wave radiation. Because most of the underlying

- 202 surface inside the PV plant is barren ground, the surface emissivity is set to 0.95 203 (Yang _et al._ 2015), enabling the LST to be deduced from (1).

- 204

- 205 **3. Results**

- 206 A statistical analysis is performed on the _in situ_ measurements, which are used to 207 contrast the natural barren site to the PV site, with the surface radiation and 208 temperature impacts from the PV plant inferred from differences between the two 209 sites. The significance of any differences is then assessed by performing Student’s _t_ -

- 210 test (Wei _et al._ 2008) on daily observational datasets.

- 211 _3.1 Surface radiative impact from the large-scale deployment of PV plants_

- 212 The SWDOWN, SWUP, LWDOWN, LWUP and NSR observed over the PV plant 213 (site A) are compared with those observed over the natural barren (site B) in Fig. 4. 214 Since annual variations may obscure more consistent local forcing from the 215 deployment of PV solar plants, the comparative analysis has been carried out 216 seasonally, _e.g.,_ in summertime (from April to September) and wintertime (from 217 October to March).

- 218 As shown in Fig. 4a and Table 1, the monthly SWDOWN observed over the PV 219 panels matches very well with that over the natural barren area (Fig. 4a). However, 220 compared with the SWUP over the barren area (site B), the SWUP over the PV panels 221 (site A) is 5.04% smaller during summertime, but 8.38% higher during wintertime. 222 Although the differences of SWUP are not statistically significant at the 95% 223 confidence level in summer (Fig. 5), the relatively energy-rich solar-radiation 224 conversion during the summertime most likely contributes to the decreased SWUP 225 over the PV panels during this period. However, the different SWUP between the two 226 sites may also result from non-linear interactions between the surface and the 227 atmosphere. Thus, even though the PV panels do convert a portion of the solar 228 radiation into electricity during the wintertime, there are certain specific factors, such 229 as the low solar elevation angle, the high inclination angle of the PV panels (34 °), 230 and the significant land-cover changes over the study area, which may be large 231 enough counterbalance the weak contribution from the solar radiation conversion, 232 resulting in significantly increased SWUP over the PV panels during the wintertime 233 (Table 1 and Fig. 4b). Since the surface albedo may be calculated as the ratio of the 234 SWUP (radiation reflected by the surface) to SWDOWN, the aforementioned time235 dependent characteristics of the SWUP and SWDOWN signals correspond to 236 different effective albedos during these two seasons (0.16 in the summertime and 0.21 237 in the wintertime) over the PV panels, which contrast to the surface albedos over the 238 natural barren area (0.17 in the summertime and 0.19 in the wintertime). Our values 239 of the effective albedo over the PV panels in Gonghe are mostly consistent with the 240 findings from Golmud (Gao _et al._ 2016).

- 241 Fig. 4c shows that the LWUP and LWDOWN values over the PV panels are much 242 lower than those over the neighboring natural barren surface throughout the whole 243 year, especially during the summertime. The decrease in LWUP values resulting from 244 the deployment of the PV panels range from 0.6 to 3.6 MJ/m[2] /day, corresponding to a 245 decrease of 8.08% and 3.64% in the summertime and wintertime, respectively (Table 246 1), are both statistically significant at the 95% confidence level (Fig. 5). The average 247 LWDOWN shows a similar behavior with a significant reduction of 7.14% in the 248 summertime and a slight decrease of 1.87% in the wintertime (Table 1 and Fig. 5). As 249 the LWDOWN values essentially consist of two components: (1) low temperature 250 radiation from the universe, filtered by the atmosphere which is relative to the 251 ambient air temperature and (2) higher temperature radiation emitted by atmospheric 252 gases, the difference in LWDOWN values (Table 1) is suspected to be associated with 253 the different air temperatures of the two sites, especially during the summertime.

- 254 The difference of the NSR at these two sites is also time dependent (Fig. 4d), with the 255 average net radiation over the PV panels significantly higher (8.20%) in the 256 summertime, and a slightly positive anomaly in the wintertime (Table 1 and Fig. 5). 257 Therefore, the PV plant serves as an energy sink during the whole year, especially in 258 the summertime. The findings shown here provide further observational evidence that 259 the deployment of PV plant does exert a surface radiative impact.

- 277 _3.2 Cooling effects from the reduced land-surface temperature_

- 278 Because large-scale PV deployments alter the radiative balance at the surface279 atmosphere interface, they may also alter the LST through the surface energy balance 280 described in section 2.4. While the LST refers to the radiant temperature of the soil 281 and vegetation at the barren site, it is a mixture of the surface temperature of the PV 282 panels and ground cover at the PV site. The deduced LST over the PV panels is 283 noticeably reduced for all months compared with those over the neighboring barren 284 site (Fig. 6).The monthly mean reduction in LST ranges from 1.8 °C to 8.2°C, with an 285 annual mean decrease of 4°C, which is statistically significant at the 95% confident 286 level (not shown here). The cooler land surface over the PV panels is related to the 287 physical shading by the PV panels, which shade a portion of the ground and, 288 therefore, reduce the heat absorption of the surface soils (Smith _et al._ , 1987). At the 289 same time, energy is removed from the PV panels in the form of electrical energy, 290 which also contributes to the lower LST of a PV plant.

291

292 **Fig. 6.** Temporal variations of the deduced LST from (1) at the site above the PV 293 panels (solid lines) and the neighboring barren site (dashed lines) from May 2015 to 294 April 2016 in Gonghe.

- 296 _3.3 Heating effect of a photovoltaic panel at 2-m height_

297 Since the surface of a PV panel absorbs solar insolation (Burg _et al._ , 2015), the 298 panels re-radiate most of this energy, resulting in long-wave radiation heating of the 299 ambient atmosphere, as noted in the introduction. We investigate the heating effect of 300 a PV panel using hourly air temperatures and the corresponding solar-panel 301 temperatures observed at site B (Fig. 1a). These hourly temperatures are first 302 combined to produce daytime (the average of values recorded from 09:00 to 20:00 303 local time), nighttime (the average of values from 21:00 to 08:00 local time) and daily 304 temperatures (the average of the whole day).The average monthly temperature 305 differences between the solar panel and the surrounding atmosphere (solar-panel 306 temperature minus the 2-m air temperature) are calculated during the daytime, 307 nighttime and the whole day, as shown in the bar graphs (Fig. 7).

308 Despite the nighttime cold surface of a solar panel (the blue bars in Fig. 7), there 309 are obvious increases in the daytime solar-panel temperatures across the whole year, 310 with an annual mean increase of 9.7 °C (the red bars in Fig. 7).The monthly solar311 panel temperatures based on daily averages of the whole observations are about 2.3°C 312 -4.6°C warmer than the 2-m air temperatures, with an annual mean increase of 313 3.8°C (the gray bars in Fig.7).The significantly increased temperature of the solar 314 panel serves as a source of heat to the ambient air, resulting in a PV heat-island effect.

- 317 **Fig. 7.** Temporal variation of the temperature differences between the solar-panel 318 temperatures and the 2-m air temperatures taken during the daytime (red bars), 319 nighttime (blue bars) and the whole day (gray bars) from May 2015 to April 2016 in 320 Gonghe (solar-panel temperature minus air temperature).

- 321

- 322 **4. Discussion**

- 323 _4.1 Climate characteristics during the observation period in Gonghe_

- 324 Based on long-term observations, from 1985 to 2016, Gonghe possesses to a typical 325 continental plateau climate characterized by strong solar radiation with long cold 326 winter, short cool summers and a short frost-free period. The mean annual 327 precipitation is 321.4 mm, with more than 88% of the annual precipitation occurring 328 in the period from May to September.

- 329 As for the local climate during the observation period (from May 2015 to April 2016), 330 the statistical results show that the cloud cover in September 2015 was 15.4% higher 331 than long-term mean cloud cover in September (from 1986 to 2015) over this area, 332 which offers an explanation for the steep drop of SWDOWN in this month as shown 333 in Fig. 4a. At the same time, most of the annual precipitation is delivered in the 334 summertime in the form of minor rain showers, which may impose a cleaning effect 335 on the PV panels during summertime. However, the long periods with less 336 precipitation in the wintertime (from October 2015 to March 2016), with the total 337 number of days of snow cover less than 10 during this long winter period, means the 338 effect of snow on the ground-cover type is limited over the study area, at least during 339 the observation period.

- 340 As shown in the wind rose of Fig. 1b, northwest or southeast wind directions prevail 341 in Gonghe. Although the two sites (A and B in Figure 1) are aligned along the 342 dominant wind direction, the effect of any temperature advection between the barren 343 area and the area with PV panels has been ignored here.

- 344 _4.2 Point measurements_

- 345 Our aim is to analyze empirically the observed surface radiative impact, as well as the 346 surface temperature changes resulting from the installation of a large-scale PV plant 347 based on parallel observations from two _in situ_ sites. Here, we use the difference 348 between the observations within the PV panels and those in the neighboring natural 349 barren area to express the change resulting from the large-scale deployment of PV. 350 The accuracy of the result depends, to a large degree, on the quality of the _in situ_ 351 measurements. As noted in section 2.1, the radiation fluxes are observed at two 352 different heights, 10 m for the PV panels and 3 m for natural barren, which may lead 353 to differences in the observed surface radiation and a bias in the comparison.

- 354 However, as the terrain in this natural barren area is relatively flat, any radiation 355 differences resulting from the elevation difference of 7 m can be ignored, which is 356 supported by the measurements of SWDOWN at both sites giving the same values, as 357 evident  in Fig. 4a and Table 1. Additionally, to minimize the contamination from 358 any other structures, such as a white box at site B, the NR01 sensors have been 359 mounted on a long cross-arm to position the sensors directly above the barren surface 360 at site B, and above a PV panel at site A. Moreover, the NR01 is a robust, research361 grade radiometer requiring only limited maintenance 362 (http://www.campbellsci.com/nr01) once the necessary instrument calibration and 363 mounting have been carried out. However, since the equipment is deployed over 364 barren areas with sparse vegetation, the outer surfaces of the radiometer and the PV 365 panel may be contaminated, so that these surfaces are cleaned every three to six 366 months. Nonetheless, most of the observed radiative difference should be 367 representative of the surface radiative variations caused by changes in the land-use 368 cover resulting from the installation of the PV plant.

- 369 As our field observations are only point measurements, our findings only represent a

- 370 single site and, therefore, may not be applicable at other sites. However, the 371 significance tests of any surface radiation differences (Fig. 5) give us confidence that 372 our findings have some amount of credibility despite the issues raised earlier. Further 373 understanding of the complex physical processes at the surface may have to rely on 374 much longer-term observations in the future. Meanwhile, the specific features of the 375 surface radiation and temperature over the PV panels revealed here can be 376 parameterized into the land-surface modules of numerical models. The possible 377 climate impacts from different installed PV-plant capacities may then be assessed 378 through a set of numerical simulations to provide a quantitative and practical guidance 379 for the rational development of the PV industry in the future.

- 380

   - _4.3 Lessons learned from the experimental design_

- 381 Although our observations reveal the impacts of the PV panel on surface radiation and 382 temperature to some extent, there is room for improvement in the design of the 383 observational experiment in the future.

- 384 First and foremost, to ensure that the parallel observations from different sites are as

- 385 comparable as possible, the observation heights should be identical. Second, the

- 386 sensor must be positioned well away from the contaminating effects of other nearby 387 structures. Third, the site representativeness is to be ensured by positioning the natural 388 surface site as far away from the PV plant as possible, while positioning the PV site in 389 the center of the PV plant if possible. Finally, the addition of other sensors would be 390 beneficial, such as an ultrasonic anemometer for the observation of any possible 391 dynamic effects, such as that resulting from the surface roughness of a large-scale PV 392 plant.

- 393

- 394 **5. Conclusions**

- 395 Although the potential climatic influences from the deployment of large-scale PV 396 plants have been well recognized based on either numerical or theoretical models, the 397 radiative impacts of PV plants and the attendant temperature changes at the surface398 atmosphere interface are still uncertain. A more realistic analysis of the impact of a 399 PV plant on the observations should be undertaken to further understanding of this 400 issue.

- 401 The parallel observations derived from _in situ_ experiments spanning two land-surface 402 types in Gonghe provide new insight into the large-scale PV effects, with the 403 emphasis on the surface radiative forcing and surface temperature changes resulting 404 from the widespread deployment of PV plants. The novel results presented here are: 405 (1) the time-dependent characteristics of the surface radiation changes with a lower 406 (higher) SWUP during the summertime (wintertime), corresponding to an average 407 effective albedo of 0.16 (0.21) in the summertime (wintertime), as well as the 408 consistent reduction of the LWUP across the whole year over the PV panels; (2) a 409 notable daytime heating and a nighttime cooling of the surfaces of PV panels. 410 Moreover, we suggest means for an improved experimental design in the future, such 411 as unified observation heights, sound installation of the equipment, good 412 representative of the _in situ_ sites, and a broader range of sensors.

- 413 It should be noted that while the findings presented here may be specific for the 414 barren area of Gonghe, the notion has not been changed that the overall radiative 415 effect from the installation of PV plants is smaller compared with the radiative forcing 416 resulting from the substitution of PV technology with fossil fuel technology (Nemet, 417 2009).
